Duration::sort¶

Back to Duration API Reference

Signature¶

Duration Duration::sort() const;

Stable Ascending Order¶

sort() returns a newly allocated one-dimensional Duration whose finite lanes are in ascending nanosecond order and whose NaT lanes are at the end. It is stable: duplicate finite values and duplicate NaT values preserve their relative source order.

Only rank-one receivers are accepted. The method does not flatten matrices or cubes because doing so would silently discard structure. Empty rank-one input is valid and remains shape [0]. The receiver is never mutated.

The implementation extracts values in logical order before sorting, so a strided one-dimensional view is ordered by the values it exposes, not by the physical order of its backing allocation.

Examples¶

Example 1. Sort finite values while placing absence last.

auto values = pluss::duration::nanos(
    {3, pluss::Duration::kNaT, 1, 3, pluss::Duration::kNaT, 2});
std::cout << pluss::duration::print(values.sort());

Output¶

Duration(shape=[6], dim=1, numel=6)
[ 0 days 00:00:00.000000001, 0 days 00:00:00.000000002, 0 days 00:00:00.000000003, 0 days 00:00:00.000000003, NaT, NaT ]

Example 2. The original remains unchanged.

auto ordered = values.sort();
std::cout << pluss::duration::print(values);

The first lane is still 3 ns; sort() does not provide an in-place form.

Example 3. An empty vector is already sorted.

auto empty = pluss::duration::nanos(std::vector<std::int64_t>{});
std::cout << pluss::duration::print(empty.sort());

Output¶

Duration(shape=[0], dim=1, numel=0)[  ]

Example 4. Higher-rank input fails explicitly.

pluss::duration::nanos({1,2,3,4}, {2,2}).sort();
// throws: Duration::sort requires rank-one input

See Also¶

  • argsort(): return source positions instead of values.

  • unique(): remove later duplicates while preserving source order.
